text:
The Supreme Court of Canada recently ruled that unapproved asylum claimants in Québec have a constitutional right to provincially-funded low-cost daycare spots.

The broader potential impacts of this ruling should set off alarm bells in every province and across the federal government. It certainly did for His Majesty’s Loyal Opposition.

And so MP Pierre Paul-Hus and I, acting as Conservative Québec Lieutenant and Shadow Minister for Immigration respectively, affirm Québec’s right to pursue the use of Section 33 of the Charter in relation to Québec (Attorney General) v. Kanyinda, should its government choose to do so.

We also call upon Prime Minister Mark Carney to direct his government to immediately review what impact Kanyinda may have on Canada’s federal immigration and social welfare programs, and outline what actions may have to be taken in order to wrest power over immigration back from Big Immigration, an overzealous judiciary, and back into the hands of the Canadian people.

The Liberals must also commit to vigorously challenging any Kanyinda-related litigation that may impact federal jurisdiction in the meantime.

Here’s why.

Canada’s asylum system should offer compassionate refuge to truly vulnerable persons in numbers we can sustainably support. But Canadians believe the asylum system should not be used as a back door by which migrants can quickly and easily end-run normal immigration selection processes. Today, the asylum system skews heavily toward the latter while preventing the prioritization of benefits to those who most urgently fall under the former.

It is the provinces that have largely been left to cover the costs of this failure of the federal government. Since the years-long Roxham Road illegal border crossing debacle began, Québec has experienced a massive spike in asylum seekers in recent years, many with unverified claims, and now hosts somewhere in the neighbourhood of 200,000. This influx, combined with the Liberals’ years-long delays in processing asylum claims, has strained Québec’s social services, including subsidized daycares.

With many Québec families already facing years-long waits for daycare spots, and with an unplanned increase in demand enabled by a dysfunctional federal asylum processing system, it’s reasonable – and frankly should be expected – that Québec would enact changes to its welfare system to ensure sustainability.

Ergo, in this specific instance, Québec shouldn’t be met with the typical reactionary pearl-clutching should it follow through with suggestions that it may invoke the notwithstanding clause.

But the impacts of Kanyinda have the potential to extend far beyond Québec’s garderies. Justice Suzanne Côté dissented from the majority opinion, saying that some of its findings had the potential to “unduly impede the state’s ability to act in the public interest by limiting the range of policy choices available to governments in designing and administering social benefits programs.” She concluded that refugee claimant status should not be recognized as what are called ‘analogous grounds’ under Section 15 of the Charter, to guarantee Charter rights.

In this, she is right.

But in the ruling, Chief Justice Richard Wagner took the opposite position, suggesting that the Charter should include asylum claimants as a protected identity group. Given the breadth of the ruling and what amounts to Wagner issuing an open invitation to the activist legal community to test the waters further, it’s not hard to imagine many of those well-paid, anti-reform lawyers salivating at the prospect of doing just that.

Nor is it a stretch that the justice’s arguments for intersectionality that the judges made in Kanyinda could be used as a test on whether unvetted and unapproved asylum claimants – particularly those without work permits – should be entitled to other taxpayer-funded benefit programs. These tests could include the legality of proposed co-pays on the Interim Federal Health Benefit, unfettered access to the Canada Child Benefit, Old Age Security, and more.

Chief Justice Wagner’s concurrence regarding recognizing “refugee claimant status” as an analogous ground under Section 15 of the Charter could also provide a hook for broader arguments against aspects of criteria-based immigration streams. This means clarity is also needed on the extent to which the Kanyinda framework could be used to legally undermine specific rules within immigration processing streams that use neutral selection criteria such as age caps, language thresholds, and education points.

Under Kanyinda, any of these criteria – the cornerstones of Canada’s immigration selection processes – could potentially be argued to have discriminatory impacts on protected or analogous grounds and, if subsequently overturned, further undermine Parliament and the government’s ability to set and enforce immigration rules.

While some may argue these scenarios are unlikely, history suggests the anti-immigration reform lobby – aka Big Immigration – will ensure otherwise. Canada’s immigration lobby is arguably one of its most powerful. While there is undoubtedly a need for vulnerable non-citizens to have their rights advocated for, a major obstacle to enacting reasonable reforms to Canada’s immigration and asylum systems has always been fierce resistance from a network of well-funded anti-reform lawyers, immigration consultants, lobbyists, and NGOs who profit off of Canada’s overly-permissive and enforcement-deficient immigration system. Big Immigration rarely, if ever, acknowledges that in order to achieve social consensus for immigration, the system cannot be left in its current state of abject dysfunction.

Big Immigration’s voices dominate immigration-related news stories and submissions to Parliamentary committees. A simple check of the lobbying registry prove they have disproportionate levels of access to senior immigration policymakers. And many individuals from this clique have gone on to occupy influential roles on the Immigration and Refugee Board or in the courts, which further dooms reform efforts.

On that note, Sean Fraser, the former Liberal Immigration Minister who bent to the will of Big Immigration to such an extent that he allowed nearly a million foreign students on work permits in a two-year period, is now Canada’s Justice Minister. The sheer volume of Big Immigration intervenors allowed in the Kanyinda case also illustrated this profound imbalance.

But given the hull-buckling groans emanating from most Canadian social welfare programs, the deep deficits most Canadian governments are running, and the disarray that Canada’s immigration system is already in, Prime Minister Mark Carney has a duty to prevent ideologically-homogenous activists from using the Kanyinda framework to block reasonable reforms or make the system even more dysfunctional than it already is.

There are many other reasons to prevent further blurring of the distinction between citizen and non-citizen using the Kanyinda framework. It will be virtually impossible for any level of government to disincentivize abuse of the asylum system if there are endless legal options for unverified claimants (or outright fraudsters) to access social services they were never intended to receive. Blurred boundaries on who is eligible to receive benefits will, beyond the obvious sustainability problems, make it even harder to prioritize those truly vulnerable groups.

For many members of the public, this lack of distinction will be perceived as a lack of fairness. In turn, there will be even less public appetite to extend social welfare benefits to asylum claimants, or for immigration writ large. Further legal erosion of the difference between citizen and non-citizen will only serve to continue to diminish the value of Canadian citizenship and accelerate the fragmentation of our already diffuse national identity.

Perhaps most importantly, Kanyinda adds a thick layer of judicial overreach to an existing spread of rulings that have already severely eroded both Parliamentary supremacy in setting immigration law and the federal government’s ability to enforce it. Changes in 2012, which prevented non-citizens who made fraudulent asylum claims from receiving taxpayer-funded supplemental health benefits (like vision care) while awaiting removal from the country, were almost immediately struck down by the Federal Court (R. v. Pham, 2013 SCC 15). This led to the now-frequent practice of judges giving more lenient sentences to non-citizens convicted of serious crimes in order to avoid consequences for their immigration status.

Parliamentary Committee testimony during the review of the immigration provisions in the current Bill C-12 suggested its reforms would immediately be challenged in court by Big Immigration. Justice Wagner’s tone in Kanyinda suggests that this lobby will be successful. Allowing this trend to go unchecked by the federal government will only further engrain the Canadian public’s sense that they are losing control, and in turn, further erode support for immigration. It will also suggest that the federal Liberals’ willingness to prevent asylum system abuse only goes so far as the court’s willingness to accept their reforms.

At present, Canadian immigration law and Canadian public support for immigration is predicated upon the principle that it is legal, fair and necessary to treat different non-citizens differently than citizens for the purposes of immigration selection and entry into Canada. This concept is reinforced by Section 91(25) of the Constitution Act, 1867, which gives Canada’s Parliament the main power to set immigration laws.

And so the public expects that they can turn to and rely on the federal government and Parliament to both support a strong Canadian national identity, manage a fair and orderly immigration system, and secure our nation’s borders. But the Kanyinda framework shows that Canada’s Supreme Court is willing to fixate on the increasingly tone-deaf voices of Big Immigration and directly challenge these foundational principles.

The Charter has a built-in fail-safe for potential extreme situations such as these, and the government and Parliament have other tools at their disposal to rein in an overzealous judiciary.

It’s now up to Mark Carney to provide clarity on how much more judicially-inspired immigration dysfunction his government will tolerate before he directs it to act.

Let’s pray that his patience has boundaries, and that the judiciary and Big Immigration doesn’t further test their limits.

title: As an Immigrant, I'm Safer in San Quentin Than If Paroled - Solitary Watch
description:
Stuck behind the cubic holes of a metal door, I was one of the many thousands of men sent to solitary confinement.
I’m treated as a person to create conditions as close as possible to life outside of prison.
The California Model has given me the opportunity to work with the San Quentin prison administration on projects that advance social justice and rehabilitation.
Being sent to CECOT is even worse than the solitary confinement I experienced here in California.
He was sentenced to life in California prison at 16 years old.
text:
The following commentary, written with the support of Solitary Watch, originally appeared as an op-ed in the Los Angeles Times on Sunday, March 15.

•

Three decades ago, I was sentenced to life with the possibility of parole in California. A lost, scared teenager, I found myself in a maximum-security prison: Pelican Bay Security Housing Unit. Stuck behind the cubic holes of a metal door, I was one of the many thousands of men sent to solitary confinement. Whenever I was taken out of the cell, my every movement was meticulously monitored. Two officers locked chains around my waist and irons on my ankles.

In these small corridors of eight cells per pod, I was taken away from the world and surrounded by a violent prison culture. Anxiety consumed me. In the abyss of isolation, my only human connections were my next-door neighbors.

I refused to give up. Unable to read or write, I picked up an English dictionary, pen and paper. I devoured books, determined to learn everything about “The Land of the Free.” The more I learned, the more I identified with my new home. I came to love my adopted country and never gave up on the possibility of a second chance — maybe even a house with a white picket fence to live the American Dream.

To be found eligible for parole, I would have to be deemed by the parole board to be rehabilitated and no longer a danger to public safety. That is the stated goal of time spent in California prisons.

Under the state’s model of “normalization,” I’m called by my name, not a number. I’m treated as a person to create conditions as close as possible to life outside of prison. The California Model has given me the opportunity to work with the San Quentin prison administration on projects that advance social justice and rehabilitation. Juvenile lifers like me have a recidivism rate of less than 2%.

All incarcerated people are apprehensive about transition to the outside world. But in my case, the prospects are so daunting that I am no longer even seeking parole. If I were freed, I would go straight into the arms of Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

In 2023, California passed Assembly Bill 1306 to prevent transfers into ICE custody once an incarcerated immigrant is granted parole or compassionate release. But Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed the bill. Since 2019, California prisons have transferred more than 12,000 people into ICE custody. The state would do the same to me if I were released.

In ICE custody, I would certainly be caught up in mass deportation to El Salvador, a nation I left behind as a 12-year-old. There, I could face yet another life sentence in an El Salvadoran mega-prison, the infamous Terrorism Confinement Center, or CECOT. El Salvador imprisons people they believe to be associated with gangs, which would include me because I tattooed myself as a teenager. Being sent to CECOT is even worse than the solitary confinement I experienced here in California. I would be trapped inside a prison system built to isolate people and destroy human connections. It is a virtual death sentence.

My older brother Gabriel is living this reality right now.

He was sentenced to life in California prison at 16 years old. After 32 years incarcerated, he was granted parole, only to be delivered into the hands of ICE. In September 2024, he was transported to CECOT.

Gabriel cannot make phone calls, receive visitors or even write to my mother to let her know he’s alive.

“They just killed my son,” exclaimed my mother over the phone. I felt powerless, gasping for air as I processed this horrible news. “I will never seehim again. He is practically dead,” she said. She also told me that if she fails to send $7 a day to the Salvadoran prison system, Gabriel, if still alive, would probably starve to death.

Trapped between California’s normalization model and CECOT’s black hole, I f ind myself between the cement walls of two distinct prison worlds.

I’m glued to my TV in the prison cell. I see ICE agents chasing brown people across the fields that they harvest to feed Americans. I ask myself: “Is this the America I learned about? Do immigrants’ lives matter?”

Malcolm X, who also learned to read and write in prison, fought against the injustice and hatred of racism, and Martin Luther King Jr. preached the power of love and the value of equality.

This is the America I learned about. In today’s America, however, real freedom is not an option for me.

text:
We break down immigration raids and related news in Southern California. Below, you'll find links and references to everything discussed in the video, allowing you to take a closer look at each topic. If you appreciate reporting like this, please consider becoming a member, buying some merch, or dropping a dime in our fundraiser so we can continue bringing you this vital information.

Have you ever wondered what the messages we get at L.A. TACO during a raid sound like? I’m going to read you a heartbreaking one from today and show you the clip. Now it’s much longer, so it's been edited for brevity.

“They were at their job site as gardeners. I drove around for fifteen minutes. Then the compa called me again and left the line open. He didn't say anything to me, but there was screaming on the line in the background. "They're taking him, help! Amy help! Don't take him! That's my dad!" It was awful. So I raced back, parked, and started filming. The dad was already in the ice vehicle. He's the only one kidnapped at this location. However, prior to this, my contact's brother was also kidnapped at their home (I believe) that morning. They didn't know for sure that it had happened since no one was around to see it, but they couldn't get in touch with him. We now have confirmation that he was indeed taken.”

ICE is still active. We’re seeing a couple of incidents on average on the weekends and an average of around seven incidents each day during the week right now, and while the quantity may be lower, the quality of these kidnappings remains brutal, inhuman, and unjust. Let’s catch you up since Friday’s post.

On Saturday, in National City, a man, a woman, and possibly a minor were kidnapped from in front of a middle school. On Sunday in Escondido, ICE agents kidnapped a man in front of an auto shop.

On Monday, we had the incident I mentioned first in this video. Another person was taken in Fallbrook in front of a food store, another father was grabbed in Lennox on Eastwood and 111th, and people continued to be taken from their ISAP check-ins at DTLA’s hidden office on Hill and 2nd.

Today, Tuesday, they were also very active, with another violent kidnapping in Paramount, where an agent brutally tackled a man inside a Home Depot, tearing his shirt and forcing him into a vehicle. In Downey, a woman was documented being kidnapped outside the courthouse as she screamed and cried. A man was also kidnapped early this morning in East L.A. ICE vehicles were present in Santa Barbara and Santa Ana today.

In Escondido, where ICE and Border Patrol activity remain consistent, three SUV’s surrounded a vehicle and took another father, leaving his teenage daughter behind. In a separate incident, unmarked vehicles believed to be ICE rammed their vehicles into another truck trying to block him in; that truck drove away, and we’re unsure if he was captured or not.

In other news, Border Patrol’s tiny terrorist, Greg Bovino, is retiring. An Afghan war veteran who helped the U.S. special forces died less than 24 hours in custody after being kidnapped while getting his kids ready for school on Friday, sparking questions. After all, we know ICE has murdered at least another detainee, that’s if you don’t count the dozens of deaths by medical neglect as indirect murders as well.

There are also horrifying reports of how our children are being treated, forced to sign as adults, subjected to virginity tests, and, in other reports, minors are becoming pregnant in detention centers and isolated from others.

I feel that when we find out the extent of the abuses not just to adults, but especially to minors and our daughters, none of us will be prepared to fully accept it, knowing many stood by when the masses could have collectively done something about it, applying relentless pressure, and fighting for these kids at least. As always, stay safe, and stay vigilant. ~ Memo Torres

title: ICE's detention expansion meets resistance in cities across the political spectrum - NPR
description:
And now, across the country, ICE is buying warehouses to house detainees.
And in the middle of it all, there's an enormous warehouse scheduled to become one of the largest ICE detention centers in the country.
It's been a deadly year for ICE detention.
In Kansas City, Oklahoma City and in smaller towns like Merrimack, New Hampshire, widespread protests have blocked new ICE facilities.
They're going to be detention facilities meeting ICE's regular standards.
text:
MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:

The Trump administration is trying to build more immigration detention centers - a lot more. Congress gave ICE $45 billion over four years to do it. And now, across the country, ICE is buying warehouses to house detainees. In many places, both Democrats and Republicans are fighting back. NPR's Jasmine Garsd went to one Maryland town to see that fight play out.

JASMINE GARSD, BYLINE: With its Civil War memorials, its rolling hills and quaint houses, Williamsport, Maryland, looks straight out of a Norman Rockwell painting. And in the middle of it all, there's an enormous warehouse scheduled to become one of the largest ICE detention centers in the country.

DONNIE DAGENHART: Did you see the building? It's huge, and 1,500 people they're trying to put in there.

GARSD: Donnie Dagenhart owns a construction company around here. He's talking about the 825,000-square-foot warehouse that ICE bought in order to hold at least 1,500 people. Williamsport has a population of around 2,000. Washington County's conservative. It voted for Trump in the last election, and in February, the county board unanimously approved a resolution welcoming ICE. That was immediately met with angry local protests. And Dagenhart says he himself has supported Trump for years, but not anymore. Among other things, he disagrees with how immigration is being enforced.

DAGENHART: I just think we're living in a police state, and it's just getting worse. They're getting the wrong people. Just get the bad ones out, right? That's what we should be doing, but they're not, it seems like.

GARSD: A similar tug-of-war is playing out in many towns across America as ICE expands its detention system. It's been a deadly year for ICE detention. There've already been 24 deaths since October, making it one of ICE's deadliest periods on record. In the last few months, activists and local governments across the country have successfully pushed back against ICE's efforts to expand. In Kansas City, Oklahoma City and in smaller towns like Merrimack, New Hampshire, widespread protests have blocked new ICE facilities. The attorney general of Maryland is suing DHS to stop the facility being built in Williamsport, citing ethical and environmental concerns. The mayor of Williamsport has been quiet on the matter. He didn't respond to NPR's multiple interview requests.

Now, for the private companies who run these centers, ICE's expansion has been a huge economic boon. During its February quarterly earnings call, CoreCivic, one of the main companies that operates ICE's detention facilities, celebrated a more than a 100% rise in ICE revenue year over year. Here's CFO David Garfinkle on that call.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

DAVID GARFINKLE: With historic funding levels for border security and an expectation of a continued increase in detention bed demand nationwide, we believe there are numerous opportunities to activate additional idle facilities we own.

GARSD: Meanwhile, in nearby Hagerstown, where the poverty rate is nearly 22% - that's twice the national average - resident Tracy Landis (ph) says that she's excited for the prospective detention center. She says the town desperately needs jobs.

TRACY LANDIS: Us American people need to take back our country. That's what needs to happen. That is opening up jobs for people. Like, let ICE do their job, and give the Americans a chance to work and have a place to live.

GARSD: Many economists say deporting immigrants does not open jobs up for native-born workers. In a statement to NPR, ICE said the Williamsport facility is expected to bring 1,125 jobs to the area and that these won't be warehouses. They're going to be detention facilities meeting ICE's regular standards. A woman named Bonnie Myers (ph), who's sitting on her porch taking in the evening breeze, is skeptical.

BONNIE MYERS: No, just the way, you know, they've been treating the people and everything. And I'd just sooner prefer it (ph) not be around here, but ain't nothing we can do.

GARSD: This is a sentiment heard a lot around here. But Patrick Dattilio with the activist group Hagerstown Rapid Response, which has fought against this detention center, says there are ways to push back.

PATRICK DATTILIO: Their power still comes from the people, and we are the people. We are the people here.

GARSD: Last week, a judge granted a temporary restraining order against this ICE facility while this whole thing plays out in court. And that means for the next few days, that massive structure will be empty. ICE can't work on it - for now.

Jasmine Garsd, NPR News, Williamsport, Maryland.

description:

In fact, without the NRPF condition, the Applicants could have paid for accommodation through Universal Credit.
Second, by taking a decision in November 2024 that she would impose the NRPF condition six months later, the SSHD unlawfully fettered her discretion.

text:
The case concerned three Tamil asylum seekers (the “Applicants”) who fled Sri Lanka for refugee camps in India, where they had faced persecution. After their boats foundered in the Indian Ocean, they were taken by British authorities to Diego Garcia in the British Indian Ocean Territory, where they were unlawfully detained for three years.

In November 2024, the Secretary of State for the Home Department (“SSHD”) approved their relocation to the UK with six months’ leave outside the Immigration Rules (“LOTR”) and access to public funds. The Applicants subsequently claimed asylum in the UK and their leave to remain was extended by operation of section 3C of the Immigration Act 1971.

After six months in the UK, the SSHD imposed a no recourse to public funds (“NRPF”) condition on the Applicants’ leave to remain. This caused significant hardship to the Applicants, who applied for judicial review of the SSHD’s decision.

The Upper Tribunal held that the decision to impose the NRPF condition was vitiated by four public law errors and breached the Applicants’ rights under the European Convention on Human Rights (“ECHR”):

First, the SSHD wrongly believed that imposing NRPF was necessary for the Applicants to obtain accommodation in the UK. This was an error of law. In fact, without the NRPF condition, the Applicants could have paid for accommodation through Universal Credit.

Second, by taking a decision in November 2024 that she would impose the NRPF condition six months later, the SSHD unlawfully fettered her discretion.

Third, the SSHD failed to take material considerations into account.

Fourth, the decision was procedurally unfair because the Applicants were not given a proper opportunity to make representations before their access to public funds was removed.

Finally, the Upper Tribunal found that the imposition of NRPF breached the Applicants’ rights under Article 1 of the First Protocol to the ECHR as it was not in accordance with the law and was a disproportionate interference with their possessions. In respect of the third applicant, the Upper Tribunal also found a Thlimmenosbreach of Article 14 of the ECHR.

Chris Buttler KC and Jack Boswell acted for the Applicants, instructed by Duncan Lewis and Leigh Day.

text:
Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) opened Sen. Markwayne Mullin's confirmation hearing with a remarkable challenge, daring the Homeland Security secretary nominee to "tell me to my face" why Paul deserved an assault that left him with broken ribs.

Why it matters: Mullin's hearing got off to a rocky start — and Paul said afterwards that he would vote against reporting Mullin's nomination out of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which he chairs.

"You have never had the courage to look me in the eye and tell me the assault was justified," Paul said, referring to comments Mullin made at a town hall, where he also called Paul a "freakin' snake."

"And while you're at it, explain to the American public why they should trust a man with anger issues," Paul added.

The other side: Mullin addressed Paul directly in his opening statement.

"Seems like you fight Republicans more than you work with us," Mullin said.

"I did address those remarks. I did explain your gimmicks by the amendment you put forth," he added.

"I don't think anybody should be hit by surprise. I don't like that. But if I do have something to say, everybody in this room knows I'll come straight to you."

"I am not scared of a challenge," Mullin said. "I am scared of failure."

"We have to get DHS funded," Mullin added, referencing the looming shutdown.

What we're watching: Paul told Semafor that while he would vote "no," he has agreed to "get an expeditious vote" on the nomination in his committee.

Still, it's clear the Oklahoma senator doesn't have an ally in Paul.

"The record should show — and I think will show — a lack of contrition, no apology, and no regrets for your support," Paul said in response.

Mullin responded: "I'm not apologizing for pointing out your character."

Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., asked Mullin whether he would prioritize the sovereignty of sacred tribal lands and open lines of communication with tribal leaders as Homeland Security secretary.

Gallego cited the construction of Trump’s border wall and patrol roads along Arizona’s southwest border during his first term. The project drew outrage from tribal leaders who said they had not been consulted by DHS before federal contractors used explosives to clear sovereign indigenous lands and burial areas to make way for the expansive project.

“The one concern I also have is that when it comes to building some of these installations on the border, there has been very little to no tribal consultation, especially with some of our border tribes,” Gallego said. “I think it’s important that we re-establish tribal sovereignty. And I hope, because of your background, you’ll understand and appreciate that.”

If confirmed, Mullin would be the first Native American to lead DHS, and only the second tribal citizen to lead a Cabinet agency. The first was former Secretary of the Interior Deb Haaland, a member of Laguna Pueblo, who served under former President Joe Biden.

Mullin swerved questions from Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., about Trump’s designs for the 2026 midterm elections, including about whether armed ICE agents will be stationed at polling places — a fear that has intensified as Trump has called for Republicans to “nationalize” elections.

“The only reason why my officers would be there [is] if there was a specific threat for them to be there, not for intimidation,” Mullin said. “I can’t sit there and guarantee hypothetically what threat [there] would be or not.”

It is a crime for military or federal law enforcement officers to be deployed to polling places.

Mullin also did not answer directly when Slotkin asked him who he believed won the 2020 election.

“Ma’am, we know that President Joe Biden was sworn into office,” he said.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., cited last week’s car-ramming at a large, Detroit-area synagogue in calling on Mullin to revamp the nonprofit security grant program — a FEMA program that provides security funding to organizations that are at high risk of terrorist attacks.

Federal investigators said the driver in the attack at Temple Israel was Ayman Mohamad Ghazali, a 41-year-old U.S. citizen originally from Lebanon whose brother and other family members were reportedly killed in a recent Israeli airstrike in southern Lebanon.

“I think the light is really blinking red, and that is the feeling for the Jewish community,” Slotkin said.

She called the program inefficient and paperwork-heavy, asking Mullin to consider a “rapid reaction fund” or other reforms.

“I would welcome the opportunity to sit down and talk to you, figure out what we need to do,” Mullin said. “I know this is very personal to you, and that’s great. We may have some differences on some some political views, but this isn’t one.”

Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., encouraged Mullin and Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., to let go of their personal feelings toward each other after today’s hearing opened with intense sparring between the two Republicans.

“I know there’s a lot of hard personal feelings here,” Fetterman said, adding, “It’s about it’s about letting it go and moving on.”

Fetterman, who suffered a near-fatal stroke in 2022, spoke about seeing disparaging comments about him while he was recovering in the hospital.

“I know there were unkind things said about me, but I can just say that it’s better to just let it all go and to find a way forward,” Fetterman said.

“That’s the time that we’re in right now in our country.”

Fetterman went on to voice his support for Mullin, though he stopped short of saying he’d vote for confirmation and acknowledged his vote could matter more if Paul votes against Mullin.

The Pennsylvania Democrat often breaks with his party on key votes and voted against shutting down the Department of Homeland Security last month.

Photo: Brendan Smialowski / AFP via Getty Images

Mullin said it should be up to the states, not FEMA, to handle disaster responses, signaling he is likely to take a somewhat similar approach to the agency as his predecessor.

“FEMA was never designed to be the first responder. That’s the states,” he said. “FEMA was designed to be the assistance to the states when the disaster reaches certain levels.”

Under Noem, FEMA aid was severely delayed for disaster victims, and the agency underwent a host of staffing issues. Noem also vowed to eliminate FEMA altogether, echoing Trump, who has long griped about the agency.

Mullin painted a less extreme, though no less vague, fate for FEMA in his testimony.

“I think it needs to be restructured, not eliminated,” he said, without elaborating on what sort of changes he has in mind.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., grilled Mullin on whether he would break with Noem on a number of immigration enforcement issues, including obtaining judicial warrants before making arrests and entering private property.

“ICE has been breaking into people’s homes without any judicial warrant. The sanctity of our homes is absolutely critical. I think you’d agree with that point,” Blumenthal said. “And the law is that a judicial warrant is required to forcibly enter someone’s home.”

Mullin said he has “made it very clear to the staff” at DHS “that a judicial warrant will be used to go into houses” and to enter “a place of business unless we’re pursuing someone that enters in that place.”

Blumenthal, citing a whistleblower report that ICE agents were instructed as part of their training to forcibly enter private property, pushed further.

“Will you commit that no longer will ICE agents or CBP agents be instructed to forcibly enter people’s homes without a judicial

warrant?” Blumenthal asked.

“Sir, I already answered this question for you. I said we will not enter home or place a business without a judicial warrant, unless we’re pursuing the individual that runs into a place of business or a resident or a house,” Mullin said.

Mullin said he made a “mistake” when he described Alex Pretti as a “deranged individual who came in to cause max damage” in an interview on Fox News soon after Pretti was fatally shot by a federal officer.

“I shouldn’t have said that,” Mullin told Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., adding, “That one, I went out there too fast. I was responding immediately without the facts. That’s my fault. That won’t happen [if I’m confirmed] as secretary.”

But Mullin declined to express the same regret for saying he “absolutely” believed the federal officer who killed Renee Good was “justified” in shooting her. He told Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., that the officer “had to make a split decision” and that there was an ongoing investigation.

Senators on the Homeland Security Committee are using Mullin’s confirmation hearing to highlight the partisan fight over appropriation for the Department of Homeland Security, which has been shut down for more than a month.

“I said to my colleague Sen. [Katie] Britt the other day that in my 14 months here, I only felt ashamed of this chamber once, and that was last Thursday, when you saw the ultimate political theater, colleagues going, ‘Let’s fund TSA.’ How about the Coast Guard? … You can’t have it both ways,” Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, said during his line of questioning.

DHS has been without funding as Democrats and the White House remain locked in a showdown over the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement agenda, which congressional Democrats have vowed not to fund until Republicans agree to a series of changes across Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol.

The White House yesterday sent its latest DHS funding proposal to Sens. Katie Britt, R-Ala., and Susan Collins, R-Maine, as negotiations yield little progress.

Photo: Chip Somodevilla / Getty Images

The questioning got off to an awkward start as Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., and Mullin engaged in a back-and-forth over their personal quarrels.

Paul said Mullin was “unrepentant” about his purported support for a November 2017 attack on the senator, who suffered broken ribs and bruised lungs. He also described Mullin as “someone who applauds violence against their political opponents” and suggested he is unfit to lead federal law enforcement officers.

“I mean, the sheer lack of any kind of self-awareness that you’re going to be leading thousands of men and women who will be — have the use of force, and there’s been great questions in our country about how that will be used, and you think a violent attack is just fine?” Paul said. “So I guess my first question is, do you think that justifying that kind of violence sets a good example for the men and women of ICE and Border Patrol?”

Mullin accused Paul of “character assassination.”

“That’s the way this game is played,” Mullin responded. “You are making this about you.”

Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., asked Mullin a question that Democrats have consistently posed to Trump’s Cabinet nominees: “If directed by the president to take an action that would break the law, would you follow the law or follow the president’s direction?”

Mullin had the same response as most, if not all, of his peers.

“The president would never ask me to do that,” he said.

Mullin again demurred when Hassan asked if he would “give the green light to lawless behavior,” as she said former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem did.

“I will operate within the parameters and the policies and the laws that you guys set for me,” he replied.

Mullin, in his opening statement, doubled down on the “snake” comments he made about Paul and refused to condemn Paul’s 2017 attacker.

“I could understand, because of the behavior you were having, that I can understand why your neighbor did what he did,” Mullin said to Paul, who had earlier pressed Mullin over his past comments that implied Paul deserved the violence he faced during an attack from a neighbor because of his voting record.

“For you to say, ‘Am I a liar, sir?,’ that’s not accurate, and I got proof to say that, because you have spent millions of dollars in my campaigns against me,” Mullin added.

Paul was displeased with Mullin’s answer, which he said demonstrated “a lack of contrition, no apology and no regrets.”

Photo: Oliver Contreras / AFP via Getty Images

Mullin urged Congress to pass a DHS funding package in his opening statement, saying lawmakers “have to realize that we’re putting our homeland and the peace of mind at risk for the American people” by not doing so.

“Sometimes it’s political theater, sometimes it’s true differences. But what we do know is that we’re playing with fire,” Mullin said. “We have 280,000 DHS employees right now that are on Day 30 without pay, and they’re still showing up every single day to do their job. That is a dedicated group of people.”

Sen. Rand Paul, the Republican chairman of the Homeland Security Committee, decried Markwayne Mullin in his opening statement for reportedly calling him a “freaking snake.”

Mullin was reportedly speaking at an event in Tulsa, Oklahoma, last month when he was asked about Paul’s votes bucking his party, leading him to say, “Rand Paul’s a freaking snake,” according to reporting from Oklahoma journalist David Arnett.

“Recently, Sen. Mullin, if you have time to listen, you were confronted by constituents that were angry because you voted against my amendment to stop all funding for refugee welfare programs,” Paul said in his opening statement. “Instead of explaining your vote to continue these welfare programs for refugees, you decided to transfer the blame. You told the media that I was a ‘freaking snake’ and that you completely understood why I had been assaulted.”

Mullin allegedly made light of the injuries Paul endured in 2017, when he was attacked in his backyard.

Typically, a Republican committee chair would be an asset during a high-stakes confirmation hearing for a member of their own party. But Paul and Mullin have long had a troubled relationship.

“I was shocked they would justify and celebrate [that] this violent assault caused me so much pain and my family so much pain,” Paul said. “I just wonder if someone who applauds violence against their political opponents is the right person to lead an agency that has struggled to accept limits to the proper use of force.”

Photo: Tom Williams / CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images

Donald Trump’s pressure campaign to persuade U.S.-allied countries to send their warships to the embattled Strait of Hormuz has not been going well.

NATO allies have balked at the request, hesitant to get involved in what is ultimately not their war. And Australia, Japan and China have refused to heed Trump’s calls for help.

That’s amounted to a shift in Trump’s rhetoric. Yesterday, during a public meeting with Irish prime minister Micheál Martin, Trump again called on NATO for help. But he quickly followed that up by saying his request is a “test” of NATO’s loyalty to the U.S., and that America doesn’t actually need NATO.

“I wonder what would happen if we ‘finished off’ what’s left of the Iranian Terror State, and let the countries that use it, we don’t, be responsible for the so called ‘Strait?’” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social this morning. “That would get some of our non-responsive ‘Allies’ in gear, and fast!!!”

It seems the president is trying a new tactic to persuade allies to help, after he’s made little progress reopening the strait alone. About 20% of the world’s oil supply must traverse the strait to reach the global market, along with tons of fertilizer compounds from Persian Gulf producers and about 20% of the global liquefied natural gas exports.

That means the prolonged closure of the waterway threatens a real affordability crisis for Trump, affecting everything from gas prices to the global food supply.

Tulsi Gabbard is likely to face persistent questions today about a classified whistleblower complaint against her that has been the subject of intense concern from lawmakers.

The complaint was filed in May, and Gabbard was required to submit the complaint to certain members of Congress within three weeks. But it took nine months to reach them due to what The Wall Street Journal described as “a behind-the-scenes struggle about how to assess and handle it.”

The New York Times then reported that the complaint was about an intercept of a call between two foreign nationals discussing a person close to Donald Trump in a conversation related to Iran. The whistleblower accused Gabbard of preventing the report from reaching spy agencies, the Times reported.

The person discussed in the conversation was later reported to be Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, which MS NOW confirmed.

When the complaint finally reached lawmakers, the intelligence report on which it was based was “heavily redacted,” according to Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., and Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va.

Gabbard, who denies wrongdoing, told lawmakers that the administration had exerted executive privilege over the intelligence report. Democrats asked Gabbard in a letter who asserted that executive privilege, when did they it and on what basis.

Photo: Andrew Harnik / Getty Images

Patel’s tenure has been defined by a string of controversies and insider accusations — namely that he has jeopardized criminal probes with his inexperience and misused his taxpayer-funded FBI jet and security detail for his girlfriend, and that he runs a “rudderless ship” as head of the bureau.

Much as it did last year, that series of alleged missteps will come up as Patel testifies before the Senate Intelligence Committee in a hearing on worldwide threats this morning.

Videos of Patel partying with the U.S. men’s hockey team after it won the gold medal at the Winter Olympics went viral last month. They drew backlash as his agency at home fielded an intrusion at Mar-a-Lago, the nationwide search for Nancy Guthrie and the ongoing fallout from the release of the Epstein files.

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are likely to press him as well on his agency’s role in domestic security planning for the Iran war.

Photo: Bill Clark / CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images

Trump’s top intelligence officials are set to testify before the Senate Intelligence Committee during its annual hearing on worldwide threats, with no end in sight to the president’s widening Middle East war.

Gabbard, an Iraq War veteran who built her political career as a critic of “regime change wars,” will be in the spotlight. The hearing comes one day after Kent, Trump’s top counterterrorism official, resigned because he could not in “good conscience” support the war with Iran, which he said “posed no imminent threat to our nation.”

Gabbard has been notably silent since the U.S. and Israel launched their joint military campaign in Iran on Feb. 28. But she is sure to face a barrage of tough questions from lawmakers after she told the committee Iran was not building a nuclear weapon during her testimony last year.

Tehran’s nuclear capabilities have been one of the only constants in Trump’s shifting justifications for striking Iran.

Ratcliffe, Patel, Lt. Gen. William Hartman of the National Security Agency, and U.S. Cyber Command and Defense Intelligence Agency Director Lt. Gen. James Adams will join Gabbard at today’s hearing.

Mullin will make his case in a committee room that’s similar to the one where Kristi Noem’s tenure began to unravel, as the Department of Homeland Security remains shut down and under scrutiny for two fatal shootings in Minneapolis at the hands of immigration officers — incidents that sparked protests and raised questions about the agency’s tactics.

Which is why lawmakers have some questions.

Not all of the questions will be hostile. Many Republicans are already primed to vote for a man who’s earned himself a reputation as both a savvy operator on Capitol Hill and as a political brawler on the Sunday shows.

For some Noem detractors, though, a change in leadership may be enough to win their approval.

“I did not feel that the management that she demonstrated as secretary met the moment,” Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, told reporters Tuesday about Noem.

“I have expressed my confidence in Sen. Mullin,” she continued. “I’ve worked with him for a while now. He’s pretty conservative, he’s pretty full-in on the president’s agenda — which is what the president would expect — but I think he’s a guy who reads very carefully not only the temperature of the Congress and what can and cannot happen, but I also think he’s connected to what people back home are saying. And I think that needs to be relayed to folks in the White House.”

Asked if there was anything she’d explicitly want to see him change at DHS, she simply said: “more engagement with the Congress.”

Read the full story here.

Joe Kent, the director of the National Counterterrorism Center, publicly announced his resignation in protest of the Iran war at about 9:30 a.m. ET yesterday. Twelve hours later, it was still on Trump’s mind.

Shortly after 9 p.m., the president posted a photo of a 2020 post Kent shared on social media in which he wrote, “@realDonaldTrump We should not sit and wait for the next attack, wipe Iran’s ballistic capability out and get our troops out of Iraq — they are only targets now. No US WIA/KIA is a tribute to the professionalism of our military and intel professionals not Iranian restraint.”

In sharing Kent’s years-old post, Trump seemed to suggest that Kent was previously in favor of launching a war with Iran, despite stating his staunch opposition to doing so in his resignation letter yesterday.

“I cannot in good conscience support the ongoing war in Iran,” Kent wrote in the letter. “Iran posed no imminent threat to our nation, and it is clear that we started this war due to pressure from Israel and its powerful American lobby.”

It’s unclear whether Kent agrees that his push for Trump to “wipe Iran’s ballistic capability out” amounted to a call for war.

Earlier in the day, Trump told reporters in the White House that he “always” believed Kent was a “nice guy” but thought he was “very weak on security.”

Markwayne Mullin isn’t bringing much experience to the role of DHS secretary, either in terms of the overall portfolio or a broader leadership position. His colleagues, per CNN, agree that “Mullin isn’t a big details guy or policy wonk.” Nor has he sat on committees dealing with the many issues that will come across his desk. Instead, it seems they’re hoping that if Mullin is merely less of a spotlight-seeker than Noem (especially without her adviser Corey Lewandowski in tow), DHS will naturally right itself.

That leaves many unanswered questions: Will the department’s social media team keep posting white nationalist messaging under Mullin? How much will he be following the quieter, but still zealous, strategy that White House border czar Tom Homan would prefer to implement? Most important, will there be any deviation from White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller’s goal of deporting as many immigrants as possible each year?

For now, Senate Democrats (mostly) are wary about Mullin taking the reins on mass deportation efforts, even as the administration turns down the volume following Noem’s ouster.

His close relationship with Trump, reportedly the closest any rank-and-file GOP lawmaker has with the president, means that he will be less likely to draw his boss’ ire than his predecessor. And for the Republicans who will rush to confirm him, that seal of approval from the White House is far more important than anything Mullin could possibly say about the policies he’ll soon be carrying out.

Read the full story here.

Sen. Markwaye Mullin may not be much of a break from the previous Department of Homeland Security secretary, Kristi Noem, in terms of immigration policy. He has appeared to embrace the hard-line immigration stances pushed by the Trump administration.

In January, Mullin defended the federal immigration officer who killed 37-year-old Renee Good, a civilian, in Minneapolis, saying the officer “had the right to defend” himself. He disparaged the ongoing DHS shutdown as “political theater” on CNN last month, as lawmakers remain at a standoff over Democratic demands for immigration reform.

And on NBC’s “Meet the Press” last year, Mullin said babies born in the United States to undocumented parents should be deported with their parents, in defense of President Donald Trump’s effort to end birthright citizenship.

“If their parents are deported, then the child should most definitely go with the parents,” he said.

Read the full story here.

title: Live: Senate confirmation hearing for Trump's DHS pick Markwayne Mullin - BBC News
description:
If you are just joining us, we’re bringing you updates today from the Senate confirmation hearing of Markwayne Mullin, the nominee for Homeland Security secretary.
Once these hearings are finished, the Senate committee will vote on whether to recommend the nominees to the full Senate.
Mullin says 'bloated' Fema needs to be reformed New Jersey's Andy Kim, a Democrat, is asking about Fema funding now.
The Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) is among the agencies that fall under DHS's purview and an agency Trump has planned to downsize.

text:
Why are confirmation hearings held and what happens after?

If you are just joining us, we’re bringing you updates today from the Senate confirmation hearing of Markwayne Mullin, the nominee for Homeland Security secretary.

He was chosen by President Donald Trump for this key government role - but as per US law, he must undergo questioning and scrutiny by senators before they vote for his confirmation.

It is part of the “advice and consent” role that the Senate plays under the US constitution, which gives the Senate the authority to review - and either approve or reject - the president’s picks.

At the hearings, the nominees are grilled by a group of senators from both sides of the political aisle about their experience and readiness for the role, as well as their views and how they would carry out their responsibilities.

Once these hearings are finished, the Senate committee will vote on whether to recommend the nominees to the full Senate. If passed, the nomination moves to the full Senate for debate and a vote, where Senators can confirm or reject the nominee.

A simple majority of 51 votes is usually required. Republicans currently hold the majority of the Senate, but some members of the party, like Kentucky Senator Rand Paul, may not vote for Mullin to move ahead. Still, Democrat John Fetterman has said that Mullin has his yes vote.

Mullin would be second Native American cabinet member in history

Arizona Democrat Rubin Gallego in his questioning notes that Markwayne Mullin would be only the second Native American in history to be a cabinet member, if confirmed by the Senate.

For those who didn't know - Mullin is an enrolled member of the Cherokee Nation, and according to his website, he is the first tribal citizen to serve in the Senate in nearly two decades.

The first Native American cabinet member was Deb Haaland, who served as Secretary of the Interior under Joe Biden.

Mullin says he respects tribal sovereignty, and he will work with nations to secure the border in a way that respects their land.

Trump's DHS nominee promises to engage with police in 'sanctuary cities'

Florida Republican Rick Scott asks Mullin about "sanctuary cities" - municipalities that limit their assistance to federal immigration authorities.

Mullin's response appears to suggest that he wants to work with the cities and leaders of sanctuary cities, who he says also love their cities. He said he would try to get in touch with sheriffs and police chiefs to see what they have concerns with.

Mostly Democrat-run cities, they have become a focus during Trump mass deportation campaign.

Mullin says he finds it "really hard to believe" that law enforcement in these communities don't want to do their job. He describes it as a "misunderstanding".

However, if officials refuse to enforce laws, then it would be hard to justify sending them taxpayer dollars, Mullin says. Cutting funding would be a last resort, he adds.

Mullin says 'bloated' Fema needs to be reformed

New Jersey's Andy Kim, a Democrat, is asking about Fema funding now.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) is among the agencies that fall under DHS's purview and an agency Trump has planned to downsize.

Kim asks Mullin if he plans to strip funding from Fema if he's confirmed. Mullin says the agency needs to be reformed.

The Oklahoma senator describes US agencies, including Fema, as "bloated".

Since Trump announced his plans to shrink the agency, Democrats have said that relief money has been moving out slowly.

Kim notes that more than 1,000 Fema grants were delayed because the current Secretary of DHS, Noem, required prior approval for grant money to go out the door.

Mullin says he won't "micromanage" the agency if he's confirmed.

Democratic Senator Gary Peters asks Mullin about foreign trips

Ana Faguy

Reporting from Capitol Hill

Ranking Member Gary Peters, a Michigan Democrat, is now questioning Mullin.

He asks if Mullin has travelled to a foreign country - outside of vacation or mission trips. Mullin says he hasn't.

Mullin clarifies that he went on a trip in 2015 or 2016, but says he did not have to disclose it to the committee because it was official.

The line of questioning appears to point at a recent Washington Post article that suggests there is little evidence to show Mullin has gone on the foreign trips he suggests he has.

Mullin goes on to speak about an official classified trip he says he went on ten years ago. He says he cannot say where he traveled because it was classified.
